items.title: The CISO’s evolving role: Protecting and defending in the agentic era
items.summary: October is Cybersecurity Awareness Month, and it’s a good time to think about how much the world has changed for chief information security officers (CISOs) in the last 12 months. A year ago, we thought we were already in the thick of AI and starting to understand it. Since then, agents have spread across the enterprise faster than most organizations anticipated. According to our Work Trend Index Annual Report , the number of active agents in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem grew 15-fold year over year and 18-fold in large enterprises. Employees are building and deploying AI systems that can access company data, interact with applications, and take actions on their behalf. These systems are built with good intentions, but even well-intentioned agents can introduce risk when access and behavior are not appropriately governed. At the same time, more people inside our companies are building with AI. Many of them haven’t written code in years, if ever, and they aren’t necessarily thinking about security the way a security team would. That isn’t a criticism. It’s how quickly the technology has expanded who can build and what they can accomplish. For CISOs, this creates two fundamental shifts. We have to protect an enterprise that increasingly operates through AI and agents. And we have to rethink how we defend that enterprise as attackers use AI to move faster and operate at greater scale. When I talk with CISOs, these are the two challenges I keep coming back to. We need to enable innovation without introducing unmanaged risk, and we need to modernize defense without losing the security fundamentals that still matter. Get the 2026 Work Trend Index report For builders: Build securely in the agentic era Cybersecurity awareness has always been about people. This year, it has to include the people building agents. If you’re a developer, a builder, or someone who has just realized that AI can help you design and build things, this part is for you. Give your agents their own identities. Where supported and appropriate, assign agents governed identities rather than personal or shared credentials. When something goes wrong, you need to know which agent did it and be able to shut it off. Protect the data your agents touch. If an agent can reach information, assume it will use it. Make sure the right data protections are in place before you connect it. And remember that the agent will not think like you. It doesn’t share your judgment or your sense of what is appropriate. If you give it access to information or systems, it will act on that access, and that can quickly become a problem. Your CISO wants you to build. They also need to know what’s being built, so they can help you do it safely. The best thing you can do for your security leader is to have the identity and data conversation early, before you build, not after. For CISOs: Protect the enterprise as agent adoption grows Your first job is to put guardrails in place so people can innovate carefully, without slowing them down. Good guardrails help teams move faster because they know where the lines are. Start with observability, and make it deep. You need to know which agents exist, who owns them, what they can reach, and what they’re doing. You can’t protect what you can’t see. Deep observability also means knowing when an agent’s behavior changes, so your team can step in before a small issue becomes a big one. Then hold people’s feet to the fire on identity and data. These are the two areas where I wouldn’t give any ground. Every agent needs a governed identity with only the access it needs, and the data it can reach needs to be classified and protected. When those two are in place, most other decisions get easier. Here’s how we’re approaching agent governance . For CISOs: Defending differently Your second job is to defend differently than you have historically done. Attackers are using AI to move faster, and our latest Microsoft Digital Defense Report shows how much that is compressing the time defenders have to respond. But defending differently isn’t simply about adopting faster tools. It’s about changing how security teams turn information into action. The more integrated your environment is, the faster you’ll be able to see an attack and respond to it. An attack rarely shows up in just one place. Signals across identity, endpoints, applications, and cloud environments need to come together with threat intelligence and organizational context so defenders can understand what’s happening and respond before an incident escalates. When your tools work together, your team sees the full picture instead of pieces of it. It also requires a security approach built to continuously assess risk, make decisions, and act at the speed threats are developing. You also need the right threat intelligence and the right partner. Threat intelligence helps organizations understand how threats are changing, which ones matter to their environment, and where to focus their defenses. Working with partners that have visibility across industries and organizations can provide broader context than an individual organization may have on its own. And you’re not going to operate at this speed without agents helping you. The same capabilities that make attacks faster can make defense faster, with agents working alongside your analysts to investigate and respond. That’s why we’re bringing integrated security operations and agentic defense together . Two jobs, one goal The pace of change over the last year has been significant, and it is likely to continue. None of this means slowing down. The CISOs I talk with want their companies to innovate. They need to protect the enterprise as it uses AI and the increasing speed of AI-enabled threats. items.summary_html:
October is Cybersecurity Awareness Month, and it’s a good time to think about how much the world has changed for chief information security officers (CISOs) in the last 12 months.

A year ago, we thought we were already in the thick of AI and starting to understand it. Since then, agents have spread across the enterprise faster than most organizations anticipated. According to our Work Trend Index Annual Report, the number of active agents in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem grew 15-fold year over year and 18-fold in large enterprises. Employees are building and deploying AI systems that can access company data, interact with applications, and take actions on their behalf. These systems are built with good intentions, but even well-intentioned agents can introduce risk when access and behavior are not appropriately governed.

At the same time, more people inside our companies are building with AI. Many of them haven’t written code in years, if ever, and they aren’t necessarily thinking about security the way a security team would. That isn’t a criticism. It’s how quickly the technology has expanded who can build and what they can accomplish.

For CISOs, this creates two fundamental shifts. We have to protect an enterprise that increasingly operates through AI and agents. And we have to rethink how we defend that enterprise as attackers use AI to move faster and operate at greater scale. When I talk with CISOs, these are the two challenges I keep coming back to. We need to enable innovation without introducing unmanaged risk, and we need to modernize defense without losing the security fundamentals that still matter.

Get the 2026 Work Trend Index report
For builders: Build securely in the agentic era

Cybersecurity awareness has always been about people. This year, it has to include the people building agents. If you’re a developer, a builder, or someone who has just realized that AI can help you design and build things, this part is for you.

Give your agents their own identities. Where supported and appropriate, assign agents governed identities rather than personal or shared credentials. When something goes wrong, you need to know which agent did it and be able to shut it off.

Protect the data your agents touch. If an agent can reach information, assume it will use it. Make sure the right data protections are in place before you connect it. And remember that the agent will not think like you. It doesn’t share your judgment or your sense of what is appropriate. If you give it access to information or systems, it will act on that access, and that can quickly become a problem.

Your CISO wants you to build. They also need to know what’s being built, so they can help you do it safely. The best thing you can do for your security leader is to have the identity and data conversation early, before you build, not after.

For CISOs: Protect the enterprise as agent adoption grows

Your first job is to put guardrails in place so people can innovate carefully, without slowing them down. Good guardrails help teams move faster because they know where the lines are.

Start with observability, and make it deep. You need to know which agents exist, who owns them, what they can reach, and what they’re doing. You can’t protect what you can’t see. Deep observability also means knowing when an agent’s behavior changes, so your team can step in before a small issue becomes a big one.

Then hold people’s feet to the fire on identity and data. These are the two areas where I wouldn’t give any ground. Every agent needs a governed identity with only the access it needs, and the data it can reach needs to be classified and protected. When those two are in place, most other decisions get easier. Here’s how we’re approaching agent governance.

For CISOs: Defending differently

Your second job is to defend differently than you have historically done.

Attackers are using AI to move faster, and our latest Microsoft Digital Defense Report shows how much that is compressing the time defenders have to respond. But defending differently isn’t simply about adopting faster tools. It’s about changing how security teams turn information into action. The more integrated your environment is, the faster you’ll be able to see an attack and respond to it. An attack rarely shows up in just one place. Signals across identity, endpoints, applications, and cloud environments need to come together with threat intelligence and organizational context so defenders can understand what’s happening and respond before an incident escalates. When your tools work together, your team sees the full picture instead of pieces of it. It also requires a security approach built to continuously assess risk, make decisions, and act at the speed threats are developing.

You also need the right threat intelligence and the right partner. Threat intelligence helps organizations understand how threats are changing, which ones matter to their environment, and where to focus their defenses. Working with partners that have visibility across industries and organizations can provide broader context than an individual organization may have on its own. And you’re not going to operate at this speed without agents helping you. The same capabilities that make attacks faster can make defense faster, with agents working alongside your analysts to investigate and respond. That’s why we’re bringing integrated security operations and agentic defense together.

Two jobs, one goal

The pace of change over the last year has been significant, and it is likely to continue. None of this means slowing down. The CISOs I talk with want their companies to innovate. They need to protect the enterprise as it uses AI and the increasing speed of AI-enabled threats.
